subject: business_studies
title: Policy, procedure or rule?
summary: Identify the kind of plan by how much freedom it leaves and whether it specifies a sequence.

facts.label: Policy
facts.definition: A broad guide for decisions that leaves room for a manager's judgement.
facts.cue: A guide leaves room to decide.
facts.case: A shop prefers local suppliers, but managers may choose another supplier when quality is better.
facts.why: The guideline allows judgement; it does not impose an unchanging sequence or prohibition.

facts.label: Procedure
facts.definition: An ordered series of steps for carrying out an activity.
facts.case: To buy supplies, first submit a request, then obtain approval, then place the order.
facts.why: The defining feature is the order of steps.

facts.label: Rule
facts.definition: A specific instruction allowing no discretion about the action required.
facts.cue: A rule does not leave a choice.
facts.anchor: allow for any flexibility or discretion
facts.case: No visitor may enter the factory without a safety helmet.
facts.why: The instruction has no discretion: the required action must be followed.

trap: Do not classify every instruction as a rule. Look for discretion in a policy and ordered steps in a procedure.

subject: business_studies
title: Attract, choose, train
summary: Separate recruitment from selection and recognise training for a specific job.

facts.label: Recruitment
facts.definition: Finding prospective employees and encouraging them to apply for jobs.
facts.anchor: stimulating them to apply for jobs
facts.case: A hotel advertises vacancies and invites applications.
facts.why: It is attracting candidates, not yet choosing among them.

facts.label: Selection
facts.definition: Choosing suitable employees from the pool of applicants.
facts.case: After interviews and tests, the hotel chooses two applicants for the vacancies.
facts.why: The pool exists; the company is now deciding who will join.

facts.label: Training
facts.definition: Increasing the skills and abilities needed to perform a specific job.
facts.cue: Training improves a specific job skill.
facts.case: A new cashier practises using the billing software before serving customers.
facts.why: The focus is skill for the current job, rather than attracting or choosing employees.

trap: Recruitment is not the final hiring decision. Training is also distinct from broader, longer-term development.

subject: business_studies
title: What makes people act?
summary: Distinguish supervision, motivation and leadership in workplace situations.

facts.label: Supervision
facts.definition: Overseeing employees' work and guiding their efforts while tasks are carried out.
facts.cue: Supervision stays close to the work.
facts.case: A shift supervisor watches the work, explains the method and corrects a machine-setting error.
facts.why: The manager is overseeing and guiding the actual work.

facts.label: Motivation
facts.definition: Stimulating people to act towards desired goals.
facts.cue: Motivation supplies the reason to act.
facts.case: A company recognises good work to encourage employees to keep improving.
facts.why: Recognition is used as an incentive to encourage goal-directed action.

facts.label: Leadership
facts.definition: Influencing people to strive willingly towards organisational goals.
facts.case: A manager earns the team's trust and inspires it to work willingly towards a shared goal.
facts.why: The emphasis is willing effort produced through influence.

trap: Real managers use several elements together. In a question, choose the element most directly described by the evidence.

subject: economics
title: Why money makes exchange easier
summary: Recognise exchange, valuation and saving functions without treating them as interchangeable.
sourceLabel: NCERT Introductory Macroeconomics, Money and Banking

facts.label: Medium of exchange
facts.definition: Money is accepted in payment, so buying does not require a matching barter partner.
facts.case: A farmer sells grain for money, then uses money to buy shoes from someone else.
facts.why: Money separates selling from buying; the shoe seller need not want grain.

facts.label: Unit of account
facts.definition: Money provides a common unit for stating and comparing values.
facts.case: A notebook is priced at ₹40 and a pen at ₹10, so their prices can be compared in the same unit.
facts.why: The amounts express values in one common monetary unit.

facts.label: Store of value
facts.definition: Money can hold purchasing power for future use, although inflation may reduce that purchasing power.
facts.case: A worker keeps some of this month's income to spend next month.
facts.why: Money transfers purchasing power across time; it does not guarantee a constant real value.

trap: Money's ability to store value is not a promise that its purchasing power never falls.

subject: economics
title: Which deficit are you calculating?
summary: Choose the correct receipts and expenditure before subtracting.
sourceLabel: NCERT Introductory Macroeconomics, Government Budget and the Economy

facts.label: Revenue deficit
facts.definition: Revenue expenditure minus revenue receipts.
facts.case: Revenue expenditure is 900 and revenue receipts are 700, in the same units.
facts.why: Only revenue items enter this calculation.

facts.label: Fiscal deficit
facts.definition: Total expenditure minus receipts other than borrowings.
facts.case: Total expenditure is 1,200; revenue receipts are 700 and non-debt capital receipts are 100.
facts.why: Borrowings are excluded from receipts; 1,200 − (700 + 100) = 400.

facts.label: Primary deficit
facts.definition: Fiscal deficit minus interest payments.
facts.cue: Primary removes past debt's interest cost.
facts.anchor: fiscal deficit minus the interest payments
facts.case: Fiscal deficit is 400 and interest payments are 150, in the same units.
facts.why: Subtract the interest payments: 400 − 150 = 250.

trap: Do not include borrowing as a receipt when calculating fiscal deficit, or subtract all government spending when calculating revenue deficit.

subject: accountancy
title: Authorised, issued or subscribed?
summary: Follow these three stages of share capital without confusing an issue with payment.
sourceLabel: NCERT Accountancy, Accounting for Share Capital

facts.label: Authorised capital
facts.definition: The share-capital ceiling permitted by the company's Memorandum of Association.
facts.anchor: authorised to issue by its Memorandum
facts.case: The memorandum permits the company to issue up to ₹10 lakh of share capital.
facts.why: This is the permitted ceiling, not an amount necessarily offered or collected.

facts.label: Issued capital
facts.definition: The part of authorised capital actually issued for subscription, including relevant allotments to vendors and memorandum signatories.
facts.anchor: including the shares allotted to vendors
facts.case: Within its authorised limit, the company issues ₹6 lakh of shares for subscription.
facts.why: It has issued shares; applications and payment are separate stages.

facts.label: Subscribed capital
facts.definition: The part of issued capital actually subscribed for by the public.
facts.case: Of the ₹6 lakh offered, subscribers take up ₹5 lakh of shares.
facts.why: ₹5 lakh is subscribed capital; it need not all be called or paid yet.

trap: Subscribed, called-up and paid-up capital are different. Money received cannot be inferred from the amount subscribed alone.

subject: accountancy
title: Current ratio and quick ratio
summary: Compare short-term resources with liabilities, then remove assets that are not quick.

facts.label: Current ratio
facts.definition: Current assets divided by current liabilities.
facts.anchor: proportion of current assets to current liabilities
facts.case: Current assets are ₹60,000 and current liabilities are ₹30,000.

facts.label: Quick assets
facts.definition: Current assets excluding inventories and other non-quick current assets such as prepaid expenses.
facts.cue: Inventory and prepayments are not quick cash.
facts.case: Current assets of ₹60,000 include inventory of ₹15,000 and prepaid expenses of ₹5,000.

facts.label: Quick ratio
facts.definition: Quick assets divided by current liabilities.
facts.cue: Quick uses the narrower asset measure.
facts.case: Quick assets are ₹40,000 and current liabilities are ₹20,000.

trap: A ratio is not a guarantee of solvency. Do not leave prepaid expenses inside quick assets.
